intro: Welcome to CSS! If HTML builds the house, CSS is the paint and the furniture. Today you'll learn how a CSS rule works, with a selector, a property and a value. Then you'll give a page about a pet dragon some color.
recap: Looking good! You wrote CSS rules that changed colors and sizes for every heading and paragraph. Remember, the selector picks what to style and the property says what to change. Next, we'll learn classes, so you can style just some things.

intro: CSS controls how everything on a page looks. In this lesson you'll learn the parts of a rule, units like pixels and rems, and how inheritance and the cascade decide which styles win. Then you'll style a band's web page.
recap: Well done. You styled a page with fonts, colors and rem-based sizes, and you know why some properties flow down to child elements. Understanding the cascade will save you lots of confusion later. Next, we'll target elements precisely with classes and IDs.

intro: What if you only want to style some things, not all of them? That's what classes are for. They're like team jerseys. Today you'll learn class selectors and rounded corners, and then you'll style a set of trading cards.
recap: Nice cards! You used a class selector with a dot to style only the cards and gave them rounded corners. Classes let you reuse the same look anywhere you want. Next, we'll learn that every element is really a box.

intro: Real pages need precise styling, and that's where classes, IDs and specificity come in. In this lesson you'll learn how the browser decides which rule wins when two rules disagree. Then you'll fix a stubborn bug on a space camp page without reaching for important.
recap: Great debugging. You fixed a specificity conflict the right way and styled elements with classes and descendant selectors. Keeping specificity low makes your CSS much easier to change. Next, we'll dig into the box model.

intro: Every element on a page is a box, even the words! Today you'll learn about padding, borders and margins, the three layers around every box. Then you'll give some squished recipe cards room to breathe.
recap: Much better! Your recipe cards have padding inside, a border around them and margin outside. Once you see the boxes, you'll see them everywhere. Next, we'll line things up with Flexbox.

intro: Layout bugs usually come down to the box model. In this lesson you'll learn how content, padding, border and margin add up, why box sizing border box makes life easier, and why margins sometimes collapse. Then you'll make a profile card exactly three hundred pixels wide and center it.
recap: Nicely done. Your card is exactly the width you asked for, and it's centered. Most developers turn on border box sizing for every element for exactly that reason. Next, we'll lay things out in a row with Flexbox.

intro: Lining things up used to be tricky, but Flexbox makes it easy. It's like arranging toys on a shelf. Today you'll learn to turn on Flexbox and center things. Then you'll put a launch button right in the middle of a launch pad.
recap: Three, two, one, liftoff! You centered the button with display flex, justify content and align items. That trick is one of the most useful in all of CSS. Next, we'll build grids, like a tic tac toe board.

intro: Flexbox is the go-to tool for laying things out in one direction, a row or a column. In this lesson you'll learn the main axis and cross axis, container properties like justify content and gap, and how items grow and wrap. Then you'll lay out a game studio's page.
recap: Well done. You built a navigation bar, a menu with gaps and a row of cards that wraps. Thinking in main and cross axes makes Flexbox predictable. Next, we'll learn CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts.

intro: Sometimes you want rows and columns, like a tic tac toe board. That's what CSS Grid is for. Today you'll learn how to make columns and add gaps between them. Then you'll turn a bug collection into a neat grid.
recap: Your bug collection looks great! You turned on Grid, made three equal columns with f r units and added a gap. Next, we'll make pages that stretch and shrink for phones, tablets and laptops.

intro: CSS Grid handles rows and columns at the same time. In this lesson you'll learn how to define tracks with repeat and fr units, place items on grid lines, and span items across cells. Then you'll build a photo wall with a featured photo and a tall one.
recap: Great work. Your photo wall has three columns, a wide featured photo and a tall photo spanning two rows. A good rule of thumb is Flexbox for rows of things and Grid for whole layouts. Next, we'll make pages responsive.

intro: People visit websites on phones, tablets and big screens. Today you'll learn how media queries change styles when the screen is small. Then you'll make three squished planet cards stack nicely on a phone.
recap: Out of this world! Your planet cards stack on small screens, and your pictures never spill out of their boxes. That's the end of the CSS course. You've finished Web Foundations, so next comes JavaScript, where your pages start to move.

intro: Most people will see your site on a phone first. In this lesson you'll learn the viewport meta tag, fluid sizing, media queries, breakpoints and the mobile-first approach. Then you'll make a hackathon page work from phone to desktop.
recap: Nicely done. Your page adapts from phone to desktop with fluid sizes and a mobile-first media query. Test at many widths, not just one. That completes the CSS course and Web Foundations, and next up is JavaScript.
